text:
Regina v. Fair

[Indexed as: R. v. Fair]

16 O.R. (3d) 1

Court of Appeal for Ontario,

Finlayson, Catzman and Carthy JJ.A.

October 29, 1993

Evidence -- Prior consistent statements -- Evidence of recent complaint not admissible at instance of Crown as exception to rule against prior consistent statements unless and until accused raises issue of recent fabrication -- Evidence of prior consistent statements by complainant may be led by Crown as part of narrative but trial judge obliged to instruct jury that statements not admitted as proof of their contents.
Evidence -- Evidence of complainant's emotional state -- Evidence of emotional trauma on part of complainant in sexual assault case admissible where Crown leads expert evidence relating emotional trauma to alleged sexual assaults -- In absence of such expert evidence, evidence of complainant's emotional state of no probative value and highly prejudicial to accused.
Evidence -- Bad character of accused -- Trial judge erred in failing to direct jury regarding limited use of such evidence.
The accused was charged with sexually assaulting, over a period of three years, the daughter of a woman with whom he was living, starting when the complainant was nine years old. At trial, the complainant testified that she initially told her aunt, her father, and her teacher that the accused was physically abusing her, but said nothing about the sexual nature of the assaults because she was afraid that the accused would beat her and her mother. Later in her testimony, she said that she discussed the sexual assaults with a friend and with a counsellor, that the counsellor told the complainant's natural father, and that her father called her mother and told her that the complainant had been sexually abused by the accused. Defence counsel objected to the admissibility of this evidence and asked for a mistrial. In rejecting the mistrial, the trial judge ruled that the evidence went to the historical background of what took place.
Evidence was also led as to four episodes of emotional disturbance on the part of the complainant. The trial judge ruled that the complainant's emotional state was relevant because it showed the effect on her of the sexual assaults.
Evidence of the accused's physical abuse of the complainant's mother was admitted. Finally, in cross-examining a neighbour of the accused who gave character evidence on his behalf, Crown counsel suggested that the accused had not permitted the complainant to play with the witness's daughter because he did not want the complainant to play with a Jewish girl. There was no follow-up to this remark.
The accused was convicted. He appealed, objecting to the admissibility of the evidence of prior consistent statements and the evidence of the incidents of emotional upset, complaining about the failure of the trial judge to give limiting instructions to the jury as to what use the jury could make of this evidence, and of the use of evidence of the accused's bad character.
Held, the appeal should be allowed.
Recent complaint evidence is not admissible at the instance of the Crown as an exception to the rule against prior consistent statements unless it comes within one of the exceptions to that general rule. Those exceptions are: (1) where recent fabrication has been raised; (2) where the evidence is part of the res gestae (a narrow exception); and (3) where it is led as part of the narrative. To qualify as narrative, the witness must recount relevant and essential facts which describe and explain his or her experience as a victim of the crime alleged so that the trier of fact will be in a position to understand what happened and how the matter came to the attention of the proper authorities. In all cases where evidence is admitted under the rubric of prior consistent statements, the trial judge is obliged to instruct the jury as to the limited value of the evidence. The fact that the statements were made is admissible to assist the jury as to the sequence of events from the alleged offence to the prosecution so that they can understand the conduct of the complainant and assess her truthfulness. However, the jury must be instructed that they are not to look to the content of the statements as proof that a crime was committed.
Before the Crown is permitted to adduce evidence of prior consistent statements to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication, it is essential that such an allegation be a live issue. Recent fabrication may be raised explicitly during the opening address by the defence, through its cross-examination of Crown witnesses or in some cases it will be implicit in its conduct of the case. The Crown should then put the court on notice that it intends to adduce prior consistent statements, and its rationale for their admissibility.
Here the Crown adduced evidence of the fact of prior consistent statements in its examination-in-chief of the complainant prior to any allegation of recent complaint having been made.
By and large, the complainant's evidence of prior consistent statements met the criteria of narrative. The double hearsay as to what the complainant said as to what her father said to her mother should be excluded, as should the statements made by the complainant to her friend and her teacher. The latter statements neither advanced nor enlarged upon the narrative.
With a proper limiting instruction to the jury, the balance of this evidence was properly admissible as part of the unfolding of events from the alleged offence to the inception of the prosecution. However, there was no such limiting instruction in this case. The jury was never told that the complaints were not admissible for the truth of their contents, and that they were to consider only the fact that the complaints were made to assist them in their understanding of what occurred and why. This was a serious non-direction because the content of the statements could be perceived by the jury as corroboration of the complainant's story.
There was nothing connecting the four episodes of apparent emotional distress with the sexual assaults. It was incumbent upon the Crown to lead an expert witness who would be in a position to relate the emotional trauma to the alleged sexual assaults. Left the way it was, it was of no probative value and was highly prejudicial to the accused. There was no direction from the trial judge as to what use the jury could make of this evidence.
The evidence of the accused's physical abuse of the complainant's mother was admissible because it was witnessed by the complainant and was one reason given by her as justifying her fear of the accused and her resultant silence about the sexual abuse. There should, however, have been a limiting instruction to the jury that this evidence should not be relied upon as proof that the accused was the sort of person who would commit the offence charged and on that basis infer that the accused was guilty.
The remark by Crown counsel to the accused's character witness raised a poisonous side issue which in no way was relevant to the charge against the accused. In his charge to the jury, the trial judge properly instructed them that there was not a shred of evidence to support this statement. However, he then gave some measure of respectability to what was done by the Crown by stating that in his view discrimination was violence. The gratuitous and unsubstantiated smear of the accused by Crown counsel should have been condemned by the trial judge, not treated as a relevant line of inquiry which fell short of being fruitful.
The cumulative effect of the non-direction in this case amounted to misdirection.
APPEAL by the accused from his conviction on a charge of sexual assault.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

FINLAYSON J.A.: -- The appellant was convicted by a jury in
the Ontario Court (General Division) of sexual assault. He was
sentenced to imprisonment for two years less one day and placed
on probation for a period of three years. He appeals conviction
and sentence.

The complainant was 16 years of age at the time that she
testified as to a series of sexual assaults by the appellant in
1985, 1986 and 1987 commencing when she was nine years old. At
that time she was living with her mother and the appellant and
the appellant's son Peter. The sexual acts complained of were
fondling in the genital area, digital penetration and one act
of forced sexual intercourse.

The trial judge permitted the Crown to lead evidence that the
complainant had made prior consistent statements relating to
the appellant's sexual abuse of her to a number of persons. He
also permitted the Crown to lead evidence of isolated incidents
of emotional upset by the complainant without having these
incidents placed in context by expert evidence. The appellant
objects to the admissibility of both heads of evidence and
additionally complains about the failure of the trial judge to
give limiting instructions to the jury as to what use the jury
could make of this evidence. The appellant further complains
about the failure of the trial judge to give instruction as to
the limited use the jury could make of evidence of bad
character. There were other grounds of appeal against
conviction, but these are the ones that I consider significant
enough to deal with.

OVERVIEW OF THE FACTS

1
. The sexual assaults

The alleged sexual assaults took place on about five
occasions from October 1985 through to February 1987. The
complainant testified that on the first occasion the appellant
came to her room when the complainant's mother was at work. He
had been drinking. He awakened her, took off her pyjamas, and
fondled her vaginal area. When the complainant asked him to
stop, he slapped her causing bruising around her eye. The next
day, the mother of the complainant noticed her bruises and
asked about them. The complainant told her mother that the
appellant had become angry at her and struck her, but she did
not tell her of the sexual assault. The mother confronted the
appellant with this slapping incident and told him never to do
that again. Later the appellant approached the complainant and
told her "just to keep her mouth shut from now on". The mother
testified at trial that the appellant had struck the
complainant on a number of occasions as a disciplinary measure.
This had been a matter of contention between them.

Other sexual assaults involved more touching and one act of
digital penetration. On at least two other occasions the
appellant struck the complainant because she resisted the
fondling. Finally, one evening in February of 1987, when,
according to the complainant, the appellant knew that her
mother was leaving the appellant because of his physical abuse
to her and the complainant, the appellant came to the
complainant's room and stated that he was going to get back at
her. He forced himself upon her and had sexual intercourse. The
next day the mother noticed that her daughter was wincing when
she took a bath. The complainant said it hurt when she went to
the bathroom. The mother examined the complainant's vaginal
area and found it to be red and inflamed. The daughter made no
other statement about her condition or what caused it.

2
. The prior complaints

The complainant testified that she told her aunt, her natural
father and her Grade 5 teacher, Murray Aikman, that the
appellant was hurting her, although she did not give them any
details. The complainant also testified that, after moving to
Saskatchewan in June 1988, she told her friend Marla Allen and
a social worker named Rose Szaba of the assaults.

The complainant's aunt testified about an incident that
occurred when the complainant was visiting her in London in May
1988 in which the complainant became hysterical. Upon calming
down, she offered an explanation to the aunt, to which the aunt
replied "some things shouldn't be allowed to happen" and that
the complainant would be safe and could always talk to her. The
precise content of the statements made by the complainant at
that time was held to be inadmissible by the trial judge on a
voir dire.

In his testimony, the complainant's natural father indicated
that he had no knowledge of the alleged sexual assaults until
it was disclosed by the complainant to a social worker in
December 1990. The school teacher, Aikman, was not called as a
witness to give evidence as to what, if anything, he had been
told by the complainant.

In the spring of 1987, the complainant and her mother moved
out of the appellant's residence. In July 1988, the complainant
moved to Saskatchewan to live with her father at which point
the complainant's mother moved in with her present husband. At
some point while she was living in Saskatchewan, the
complainant testified that she told a friend she had met in
school, Marla Allen, about the assaults although Allen was not
called to testify.

In 1990 the complainant and her father began seeing a social
worker with the Social Services Department named Rose Szaba to
obtain help with problems they had been having in
communicating. The complainant testified that Szaba had to ask
the complainant a number of questions concerning her past for
the Department. One of the questions was whether the
complainant had been sexually abused, to which the complainant
answered "yes". After questioning her further, Szaba contacted
the police and the complainant's father. The appellant was
subsequently charged with sexual assault.

3
. The complainant's emotional state

The evidence of the complainant's emotional state during the
period of the alleged assaults came mainly from the testimony
of the complainant's aunt and the complainant's mother. The
aunt testified to four specific instances in which she recalled
the complainant's emotional state had been abnormal.

(a) During a visit around Christmas 1986 to the appellant's
home, in which the complainant and her mother were living,
the complainant appeared very nervous, withdrawn and timid,
and would follow her around and "cling" to her.

(b) In May 1988 while the complainant visited her aunt in
London, Ontario she, her aunt, and her aunt's fiance drove
to a video store to rent a movie. The complainant got out
of the car in a daze, walked to the end of the strip mall,
and sat down on the curb and started to rock and cry. She
was speaking in a very low tone of voice and became more
and more upset to the point of becoming hysterical. This
lasted for about 45 minutes.

(c) In November of 1989, the complainant called her aunt from
Hamilton to see if she could come to London for a visit.
She appeared upset over the phone and wished to take the
bus leaving in 20 minutes. The aunt picked the complainant
up at the bus station, and the complainant seemed very
quiet, distraught and withdrawn.

(d) Approximately a week and a half after the last visit, the
aunt received a call from the complainant from the London
bus station. When the aunt picked her up from the station,
the complainant was standing in the middle of the sidewalk
with her head down and crying. She was very despondent and
would not talk for hours. During the visits to London, the
complainant would work all through the night cleaning and
would rarely get to sleep before 4:00 or 5:00 in the
morning. She would sleep late into the day, get up
despondent and depressed, and the same cycle would begin
again.

The complainant's mother also testified as to the
complainant's emotional state during the relevant period. She
testified that the complainant, who used to be very outgoing,
became withdrawn and introverted and had no self-esteem. She
also testified that after she and the complainant moved out of
the appellant's home, she noticed that the complainant's
sleeping habits had changed, and that she had problems sleeping
so that she would sometimes sit awake until 3:00 or 4:00 in the
morning.

The complainant's father gave evidence as to the emotional
state of the complainant both before and after the disclosure
to Szaba of the assaults. He testified that, during the
complainant's stay in Saskatchewan in 1988 "she seemed to be
showing signs of not dealing with things well. She was
despondent; she was depressed. Emotionally she seemed as if she
was having a good deal of difficulty but couldn't come to terms
with it." He also testified that after the complainant had
disclosed the assaults to the social worker in December of 1990
the complainant became a totally different person, was
depressed and was having difficulty dealing with the situation
to the point of not being able to complete her last three weeks
of Grade 9 and dropping out of school the next year.

Issue 1. Evidence of prior consistent statements of sexual
abuse

In R. v. Jones (1988),
1988 CanLII 7142 (ON CA)
, 44 C.C.C. (3d) 248 at p. 255, 66 C.R.
(3d) 54, this court restated the common law rule that
evidence of prior consistent statements made by a witness are
generally speaking not admissible as evidence of the
consistency of such witness. It is generally accepted that the
rationale for this rule relates to concerns about hearsay and
the probative value of such evidence. In R. v. Campbell (1977),

1977 CanLII 1191 (ON CA)
, 17 O.R. (2d) 673 (C.A.) at p. 685, 38 C.C.C. (2d) 6 at p. 18,
Martin J.A. stated:

The refusal of the trial Judge to admit the evidence of
other witnesses, whether in cross-examination or otherwise,
of previous statements made by the appellant, involves two
separate rules of evidence:

I. The rule which precludes an accused from eliciting from
witnesses self-serving statements which he has
previously made.

II. The rule which provides that a witness, whether a party
or not, may not repeat his own previous statements
concerning the matter before the Court, made to other
persons out of Court, and may not call other persons to
testify to those statements.

Statements made by an accused which infringe rule I are
exluded as hearsay. The narration by a witness of earlier
statements made to other persons out of Court appears to be
excluded under rule II, because of the general lack of
probative value of such evidence, save in certain
circumstances, in support of the credibility of the witness.

Wigmore on Evidence (Chadbourne rev. 1972), vol. 4, at p. 255,
para. 1124, describes the second reason for the rule:

When the witness has merely testified on direct examination,
without any impeachment, proof of consistent statements is
unnecessary and valueless. The witness is not helped by it;
for, even if it is an improbable or untrustworthy story, it
is not made more probable or more trustworthy by any number
of repetitions of it. Such evidence would ordinarily be
cumbersome to the trial and is ordinarily rejected.

This rule is subject to certain exceptions. With the
abrogation of the rules relating to evidence of recent
complaint in sexual offences by
s. 275
of the
Criminal Code,
R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46
(the "Code"), the two exceptions that
could have application to this case are (1) where recent
fabrication is alleged and (2) where the previous consistent
statement is admitted as part of the res gestae or part of the
narrative. As to these two heads, the court in Jones stated at
p. 256:

With respect to recent fabrication, it is clear that there
was no basis for Crown counsel to lead evidence of a prior
consistent statement of the complainant on that basis as Mrs.
H. was the first witness called. She had not yet been cross-
examined at the time that the evidence of the recent
complaint was adduced. There was no basis upon which the
trial judge could find that the accused had alleged or would
allege recent fabrication with respect to any of
complainant's evidence which, of course, had not yet been
given. It was clearly not admissible on that basis as an
exception to the general rule.

It is equally clear that the evidence was not admissible as
an exception under category No. 2. The complaint was made
four days after the event and in the circumstances of this
case it is not suggested that it formed part of the res
gestae. Nor were the details of the alleged assault necessary
as part of the narrative of the case. At best, the Crown was
entitled to lead evidence from Mrs. H. that as a result of
information she received from her daughter on the Wednesday,
she contacted the police. To that extent only, it may have
been admissible as part of the narrative. The question and
answer which I have set forth above makes it quite clear that
the evidence was adduced by counsel for the Crown to show
consistency on the part of the complainant whom he would
later call as witness. It was inadmissible for this purpose.
The fact that defence counsel failed to object to its
admission does not remedy the error.

The Crown in this case led the following evidence from the
complainant in chief:

PART I

Q. Now I think in light of your saying that, that is
something I am going to want to talk to you about.
You've indicated to the ladies and gentlemen the events
that you say happened to you, including the last
incident which you tell us was an act of sexual
intercourse. During those events taking place and up
until the point in time you were in the bathroom with
your mother, why is it that you feel that it wasn't
necessary to tell at least your mother?

A. I knew what he was doing to me was wrong and I wanted to
tell my mom I was scared.

Q. What were you afraid of?

A. I was afraid of Jack hurting us because I watched him
beat my mom up and he used to do that to me too.

Q. Did you tell anybody about this?

A. I told my aunt and my dad that Jack was physically
abusing me, and I remember telling a teacher -- my
grade five teacher -- that Jack was hurting me.

Q. Did you give him any details?

A. No.

Q. Why not?

A. Because I didn't know what Jack would do. Because I knew
if I said anything they would have to tell somebody.

Q. Who would have to tell somebody?

A. Whoever I told.

And later on, with reference to her return to Saskatchewan:

PART II

Q. When you were back in school did you have a friend, like
a best friend or somebody?

A. Yes.

Q. Who was that?

A. I had lots of friends at school.

Q. Did you ever talk to any of them about this?

A. After I have moved out west I did.

Q. Who did you talk to?

A. My friend Marla.

Q. What is Marla's last name?

A. Allen.

Q. Why did you choose her?

A. She was pretty quiet. She was really nice to me 'cause
it was my first year out west and I was in grade seven.
She was one of the first people who became my friend
out there.

Q. At some point in time once, as you say, you moved out
west, did you meet with any professional people who
might be able to give you some help, and if you did why
did you decide to do that?

A. I did meet with a counsellor.

Q. What was the reason for that?

A. My dad and I weren't talking much because he noticed
that I was really different and I didn't want to talk,
and so we went to counselling so we could work on our
communication and sometimes we went together and
sometimes we went by ourselves to see the counsellor.

Q. Did you ever make the decision as to how you should
handle these events and who you should talk to about
it?

A. No, I never thought about telling anyone, but -- telling
anyone that would have to report it to someone. And one
day I was in my counsellor's office and she had to ask
me a number of questions about my past for the
department of social services and she asked me if I had
been sexually abused, and I just looked at her and I
said "yes".

Q. Did you talk to this person about this?

A. Yes, I did.

Q. Who was that?

A. Her name was Rose Szaba.

Q. Without going into detail again about what you told Rose
Szaba, what did Miss Szaba decide to do or did you
decide to do? Did you talk to any police for example?

A. Rose Szaba reported it to the police.

Q. Where?

A. In Regina. That was on the Friday afternoon and we made
an appointment with Sergeant Affie (ph) for Monday
morning.

Q. Who is he? He is a policeman where?

A. In Regina.

Q. What did you do?

A. I went in and I talked to him for awhile about being
abused and then I had to write a statement of what
occurred when I was living at Mr. Fair's house.

Q. At this point in time -- maybe we can confine it prior
to the trial starting. What would you say as to the
effect that this has had on you now?

A. My dad and I aren't very close any more. He had a lot of
trouble dealing with it because it's hard for him to
understand how I feel. And I haven't lived at home
since this time last year because I couldn't talk to
-- I couldn't talk to my dad.

Q. When did you tell your father that this had happened?

A. Rose Szaba told him the same day.

Q. And have the two of you tried to talk about it? Have you
tried to talk to your father about it?

A. I tried to talk to him about coming to counselling with
me to see my therapist so he can understand how I feel
and so he can help me deal with all of this.

Q. Did you at any point in time decide that this is
something you should talk to your mother about?

A. The day I disclosed to Rose Szaba, my dad called my mom
and told her that I had been sexually abused while we
were living at Jack's and that Jack was the person who
abused me.

Defence counsel at trial objected to the admissibility of
this evidence and asked for a mistrial. In rejecting the
mistrial, the trial judge ruled as follows:

This is an application for a mistrial by defence counsel on
the Crown's hearsay evidence which came through the
complainant that tended to show there were prior consistent
statements on the part of the complainant, with respect to
complaints that the complainant made to her father, her aunt,
and others including the police officers.

The defence argues it is not admissible because there has
been no suggestion at this point in the evidence of recent
concoction by the defence. That it could, on the defence
position, only bolster the evidence.

I rule there is no mistrial in respect to that evidence. It
goes to the historical background of what took place. It is
proper for that purpose to outline to the jury what the
background was.

There is also a suggestion, I understand from the Crown,
that there may be a witness called by the defence to whom the
witness made a complaint; one Rose Szaba. I am satisfied on
the historical significance of the alleged sexual offence
that the evidence is proper. If there are any problems I can
discuss that issue in my jury charge.

(Emphasis added)

I have separated the two extracts from the transcript and
identified them as Parts I and II for ease of reference. Part I
is evidence relating to why there was not a recent complaint as
to the sexual assaults while Part II is the evidence as to when
such a complaint was finally made. Part I statements were not
admissible in the period prior to the passage of the
predecessor to
s. 275
of the
Code
because only a complaint made
at the first reasonable opportunity was admissible to avoid the
permissive inference that the failure to make a complaint tells
against the truthfulness of the complainant's evidence and is
relevant to her credibility. The trial judge, on a voir dire to
determine admissibility, might well hear an explanation as to
why a complaint was not made or why it was late, but his ruling
would only permit or reject the admission of the complaint. If
the complaint was ruled admissible, the jury would not have the
benefit of the evidence given on the voir dire as to what
influenced the complainant to hesitate to complain in a timely
fashion: see R. v. Kistendey (1975),
1975 CanLII 1402 (ON CA)
, 29 C.C.C. (2d) 382 (Ont.
C.A.), and particularly Dubin J.A. at p. 390.

Section 275
of the
Code
finds its origin in s. 246.5 of S.C.
1980-81-82-83, Vol. III, c. 125, passed on August 4, 1982, and
proclaimed in force on January 4, 1983. It read:

246.5 The rules relating to evidence of recent complaint in
sexual assault cases are hereby abrogated.

The word "abrogate" is a curious one for the Parliament of
Canada to use, but it appears to be a word of some precision
and antiquity. According to Jowitt's Dictionary of English Law,
2nd ed. (1977), abrogation means:

. . . the act of annulling: the repeal of a law. It stands
opposed to rogation: it is distinguished from derogation,
which implies the taking away only some part of a law; from
subrogation, which denotes the adding a clause to it; from
obrogation, which implies the limiting or restraining it;
from dispensation, which only sets it aside in a particular
instance; and from antiquation, which is the refusing to pass
a law.

To understand what rules have been abrogated, it is necessary
to explore the underlying basis of the law prior to the
effective date of the amendment. Evidence of recent complaint
was admissible as an exception to the common law rule that a
witness's testimony-in-chief may not be buttressed by the party
calling her by proving that she made a prior consistent
statement (by asking her or otherwise): see R. v. Timm,
1981 CanLII 207 (SCC)
, [1981]
2 S.C.R. 315 at p. 321, 59 C.C.C. (2d) 396 at p. 402. The
classic statements of the exception are contained in R. v.
Lillyman,
[1896] 2 Q.B. 167
, [1895-9] All E.R. Rep. 586
(C.C.R.), and R. v. Osborne,
[1905] 1 K.B. 551
, [1904-7] All
E.R. Rep. 84 (C.C.R.). The evidence of the complainant is
admissible only upon the ground that it is a complaint of that
which is charged against the accused and can legitimately be
used only for the purpose of enabling the jury to judge for
themselves whether the conduct of a woman who claims to have
been subjected to a sexual attack was consistent with her
evidence given under oath in the witness stand negativing
consent, and affirming the acts complained of were against her
will, and in accordance with the conduct they would expect of a
truthful woman under the circumstances detailed by her.

The emphasis of the exception was on the statement being
admissible, not merely to negative consent, but because it was
consistent with the story of the complainant. As such it was
the fact of the complaint that was significant, not the detail
of it, and accordingly it could not be introduced as evidence
of the truth of its content. The downside of not having such
evidence was that the trial judge was obliged to instruct the
jury that they could draw an adverse inference as to the
truthfulness of the complainant's story: see additionally R. v.
Boyce (1974),
1975 CanLII 569 (ON CA)
, 7 O.R. (2d) 561, 23 C.C.C. (2d) 16 (C.A.). The
substance of the above was adopted by Lamer J., speaking for
the Supreme Court of Canada, in Timm, supra, where he stated at
pp. 321-22 S.C.R., p. 402 C.C.C.:

That exception was recognized as necessary to negate the
adverse effect the alleged victim's silence might have on her
credibility when relating the circumstances of the offence
and, if essential to the commission of the offence or simply
averred by the victim, the victim's credibility when
asserting absence of consent: R. v. Lillyman, supra; R. v.
Osborne, supra; Thomas v. The Queen (1952),
1952 CanLII 7 (SCC)
, 103 C.C.C. 193 at
pp. 200-1, [1952] 4 D.L.R. 306 at pp. 212-3, [1952] 2 S.C.R.
344 at p. 355. That possible adverse effect is predicated
upon the assumption that the true victim of a sexual offence
will, under normal circumstances, complain at the first
reasonable opportunity. Early complaint evidence seeks to
negate the inference that could otherwise be drawn from the
victim's silence as a result of that assumption.

The objection to the rule was that it placed a woman who had
been subjected to a sexual assault in a special category where
it was incumbent upon her to demonstrate that she had acted in
the manner expected of a truthful woman who had in fact been
sexually violated. Failure to conform to this standard could be
reason enough for disbelieving her. This is a burden not placed
on victims of any other crime and the standard, if it was ever
valid, has no validity in modern society.

Now what is the effect of the abrogation of this exception to
the rule against past consistent statements? Since the
exception was only applicable in sexual offences, and only to
the case-in-chief for the Crown, surely the consequence of
abrogation must be that evidence of recent complaint by the
complainant is no longer admissible as part of the Crown's case
when sexual offences enumerated in the present
s. 275
of the

Code
are alleged. This is a result which probably was not
anticipated by the proponents of the abrogation of the rule
against recent complaint because it has resulted in the Crown
being unable to lead this evidence, where it exists, to show
consistency on the part of the complainant and rebut the
possible adverse inference referred to by Lamer J. in Timm,
supra, that her allegations are untrue.

On the other hand, there never was a prohibition against the
accused attempting to exploit the lack of a recent complaint,
and since only the right of the Crown to lead the evidence-in-
chief has been negated, the defence can elect whether to
open this door or not. In the result, if prior consistent
statements are to be admissible as part of the Crown's case-in-
chief, they cannot qualify as recent complaints and can only
be admissible by meeting the test in Jones, supra: (1) where
recent fabrication is alleged or (2) as part of the res gestae
or the narrative.

Recent fabrication. This is a favourite justification of the
Crown for leading evidence of prior consistent statements, but
too often, as in the case under appeal, the questions are put
to the complainant before the record indicates such an attack
is to be made, much less that it has been. Here the defence
counsel objected promptly and the trial judge ruled that the
statements were admissible as part of the narrative, stating
that "[i]t goes to the historical background of what took
place". The trial judge also (and quite incorrectly) relied
upon the Crown's suggestion that the defence might call Szaba
as a witness, something which was not done.

The Crown, in this court, attempted to bolster this ruling by
pointing out that the defence had expounded at length on this
evidence and had tried to capitalize upon what the defence
perceived as contradictions in the various statements made by
the complainant. Thus it was submitted that the evidence is
admissible, albeit ex post facto, in order to rebut a defence
of recent fabrication. However, this is another reason why the
basis of the admissibility of the evidence should be
established at the earliest possible moment. Once defence
counsel had failed in his objection to the admissibility of the
statements, he was obliged to put the best face on the
situation. Two legitimate areas of exploration were the
lateness of the specific complaint about sexual abuse and the
fact that the complainant had been less than forthcoming about
the circumstances giving rise to her bruises and vaginal
inflammation when asked about them by her mother.

In my opinion, if the Crown is relying upon recent
fabrication as the basis for the admissibility of prior
consistent statements, it must wait until the defence has
clearly opened this door by making an opening statement, or
through cross-examination of the complainant or other Crown
witnesses or, as in R. v. Owens (1986),
1986 CanLII 4690 (ON CA)
, 33 C.C.C. (3d) 275, 55
C.R. (3d) 386 (Ont. C.A.), by the allegation of fabrication
becoming implicit from the defence's conduct of the case. If
this door is opened during cross-examination, questions
directed to refuting the allegation can be asked in re-
examination or, if necessary, by calling or recalling
witnesses. This involves little extra time and avoids the
problem of the court having to consider a mistrial and the
consequence of putting the youthful complainant through the
experience of testifying again. When the justification for the
evidence is to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication, the
Crown should announce to the court that that is the reason it
is being led so that the trial judge is aware of this problem
from the outset and defence counsel is firmly on notice.
Another caveat: it is only consistent statements made prior to
the time when it is alleged that the fabrication began that are
admissible.

Res gestae. This is a phrase used in the law of evidence to
explain the admissibility of words used by a person that shed
light upon the quality of the act they accompany. The words are
considered to be so inter-related to a fact in issue that they
become a part of the fact itself. To qualify, the words must
introduce the fact in issue, explain its nature, or form in
connection with it one continuous transaction: see Jowitt's,
supra. I do not regard res gestae as a fertile area for
enlarging the admissibility of prior consistent statements.
This court attempted that in R. v. Khan (1988),
1988 CanLII 7106 (ON CA)
, 42 C.C.C. (3d)
197 at pp. 207-12, 64 C.R. (3d) 281, but this approach was not
approved by McLachlin J. in the Supreme Court of Canada: see R.
v. Khan,
1990 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 531, 59 C.C.C. (3d) 92.

Khan was a case in which a girl who was four-and-a-half years
old at the time of trial was unable to testify as to a sexual
assault on her by a physician when she was three-and-a-half
years old. The trial judge would not permit her to testify
because of her tender years and he refused to admit into
evidence a statement that she made to her mother some 15
minutes after she left the physician's office. This court, in
reversing the trial judge, held that it was admissible as a
spontaneous declaration made under the stress or pressure of a
dramatic or startling event. However, McLachlin J., speaking
for the Supreme Court of Canada, was not prepared to enlarge
res gestae as an exception to the hearsay rule, despite
acknowledging "the need for increased flexibility in the
interpretation of the hearsay rule to permit the admission in
evidence of statements made by children to others about sexual
abuse" (p. 543 S.C.R., p. 102 C.C.C.). Instead, in affirming
this court's decision to order a new trial, she opted for the
policy "that hearsay evidence of a child's statement on crimes
committed against the child should be received, provided that
the guarantees of necessity and reliability are met" (p. 548
S.C.R., pp. 105-06 C.C.C.). The statement of the child to the
mother as to what had occurred in the physician's office was
the critical evidence of the sexual assault, and it was
admitted for the truth of its contents. Thus, the "necessity
and reliability" test became an exception to the hearsay rule,
not an exception to the use of prior consistent statements
which, as noted earlier, are inadmissible on the basis of a
combination of hearsay and lack of probative value.

Dr. Khan was subject to disciplinary proceedings by his
profession with respect to the same facts that resulted in his
prosecution. Those proceedings resulted in appeals which
culminated in a hearing before the Ontario Court of Appeal
after the Supreme Court of Canada released its decision in
Khan. At the disciplinary committee, the out-of-court statement
by the child to her mother was admitted into evidence and in
addition the complainant, who was then eight, testified. In
Khan v. College of Physicians & Surgeons of Ontario (1992),
1992 CanLII 2784 (ON CA)
, 9
O.R. (3d) 641, 76 C.C.C. (3d) 10, this court upheld this
procedure. Doherty J.A., for the court, stated at p. 657 O.R.,
p. 24 C.C.C.:

The fact that the child testifies will clearly impact on
the necessity of receiving his or her out-of-court statement.
Necessity cannot, however, be equated with unavailability. In
Khan, McLachlin J. instructs us that necessary means
"reasonably necessary" (at p. 546 S.C.R., p. 104 C.C.C.).
In the context of cases involving an alleged sexual assault
on a child, reasonable necessity refers to the need to have
the child's version of events pertaining to the alleged
assault before the tribunal charged with the responsibility
of determining whether the assault occurred. In my view, if
that tribunal is satisfied that despite the viva voce
evidence of the child, it is still "reasonably necessary" to
admit the out-of-court statement in order to obtain an
accurate and frank rendition of the child's version of the
relevant events, then the necessary criterion set down in
Khan is satisfied: see Anne McGillivray, "R. v. Laramee
: Forgetting Children, Forgetting Truth"
(1991), 6 C.R. (4th)
325 at pp. 335-41
.

The same criteria of necessity are not present in the case on
appeal and I do not think it essential to the jury's full
understanding of this case that the principles of Khan be
applied.

Narrative. It seems to me that the court should look to
narrative as an exception to the rule against the admission of
previous consistent statements for a more hopeful approach to
this vexing problem of the evidence of children in sexual
assault cases. It must be a part of the narrative in the sense
that it advances the story from offence to prosecution or
explains why so little was done to terminate the abuse or bring
the perpetrator to justice. Specifically, it appears to me to
be part of the narrative of a complainant's testimony when she
recounts the assaults, how they came to be terminated, and how
the matter came to the attention of the police.

This approach has been accepted by courts of appeal in this
province and in others. In R. v. Owens, supra, Lacourcière J.A.
stated at pp. 278-79:

The appellant's submission is that the learned trial judge
erred in placing reliance upon their previous consistent
statements in assessing the credibility of the youthful
witnesses. There is no complaint made concerning the
admission of the boys' statements to their parents. The
abrogation of the rule relating to evidence of recent
complaint in sexual assault cases by s. 246.5 of the
Criminal
Code
, which came into force on January 4, 1983, does not have
the effect of rendering evidence of such complaints
inadmissible in all cases. In certain circumstances the
statement may be an important part of the narrative: R. v.
George (1985),
1985 CanLII 657 (BC CA)
, 23 C.C.C. (3d) 42, or may be admissible to
show the witnesses' consistency of position: R. v. Page
(1984),
1984 CanLII 3470 (ON HCJ)
, 12 C.C.C. (3d) 250 at p. 254, 40 C.R. (3d) 85.

(Emphasis added)

In an earlier case, R. v. Cassibo (1982),
1982 CanLII 1953 (ON CA)
, 39 O.R. (2d) 288,
70 C.C.C. (2d) 498 (C.A.), the court was dealing with an
appellant who had been convicted of incest involving his two
daughters. The Crown elicited from the victims that acts of
intercourse with the appellant ceased when the victims made a
complaint to their mother. The mother testified and denied that
the complaints had been made. The court held that the
complaints were admissible as recent complaints and the fact
that the complainants' evidence with respect to what they had
told their mother was denied by her was no reason for excluding
the complaints. However, Martin J.A. for the court stated at p.
297 O.R., p. 509 C.C.C.:

There is another aspect of this case. The Crown, in my
view, was duty bound to disclose the entire picture and to
adduce the evidence in its possession that the alleged
improprieties ceased some time before the charges were laid.
The obvious question would then be why had they ceased. I do
not think Crown counsel in the particular circumstances of
this case could have been prevented from adducing evidence
from the complainants that the appellant's sexual activities
towards them ceased because their mother after a certain
point did not leave them alone with their father. That
evidence, if it had been adduced, would naturally have raised
a question in the mind of the trier of fact as to why their
mother at a certain point took that precaution. There could
only be two answers: (1) that the mother had personal
knowledge of what was occurring, or (2) that Rosetta and
Darlene had told her about the appellant's conduct. The
Crown, it seems to me, was required to adduce evidence to
show the reason for the cessation of the matters complained
of. In the peculiar circumstances of this case the evidence
of what the girls had told their mother was so inextricably
interwoven with their evidence that the case could not have
been properly presented to the court without admitting this
evidence. For these reasons also I would hold that the
admission of the complaints was not an error and, in any
event, did not result in a substantial wrong or a miscarriage
of justice.

(Emphasis added)
The narrative exception has also been accepted by the British
Columbia Court of Appeal in R. v. George (1985),
1985 CanLII 657 (BC CA)
, 23 C.C.C. (3d)
42, in which MacFarlane J.A. stated at p. 45:

Such evidence, in those unusual circumstances, was
admissible, not as a recent complaint to show consistency of
conduct, but because it was an important part of the
narrative in the case. The trial judge told the jury that the
evidence was advanced on that basis. He told them that it was
not evidence of the truth of the matter. He told them also
that that they might consider that the "evidence showed a
certain consistency of conduct on her part, but nothing
more". If that direction means that the jury could properly
consider the conduct of the girl, but not use the evidence to
establish the truth of what she had said, then I see no harm
in the direction. But what was missing was a direction as to
the limited purpose of the evidence in question.

In addition, the admission of the previous consistent
statements in this case takes into account the rationale for
the rule prohibiting the admissibility of such statements.
First, as noted in George, the complaints are not admissible
for the truth of their contents, but only for the fact of their
existence. In those circumstances, it is not necessary for the
jury's understanding of the unfolding of events that it be
apprised of the content of the statements made although it is
always open to the defence to explore the content if it feels
that this will be to the advantage of the accused. Unless the
nature of the complaint becomes controversial at the instance
of the defence, it is not what the complainant says that is
important, but the fact that she said it. Since these out-of-
court statements are not admissible to prove the truth of
their contents, they are not considered hearsay and the first
aspect of the rationale for the inadmissibility of out-of-court
statements does not apply.

The second aspect of the rationale for the rule against
admitting previous consistent statements is that such evidence
has little, if any, probative value. However, narrative is
justified as providing background to the story -- to provide
chronological cohesion and eliminate gaps which would divert
the mind of the listener from the central issue. It may be
supportive of the central allegation in the sense of creating a
logical framework for its presentation -- but it cannot be
used, and the jury must be warned of this, as confirmation of
the truthfulness of the sworn allegation.

In admitting the prior consistent statements in these
circumstances, I find comfort in another decision of Doherty
J.A. in R. v. Toten (1993),
1993 CanLII 3427 (ON CA)
, 14 O.R. (3d) 225, 82 C.C.C. (3d) 5
(C.A.), delivered on behalf of a panel of five judges. The
court was concerned with the constitutionality of
s. 715.1
of
the
Code
authorizing out-of-court videotaping of statements by
youthful victims of specified offences. In rejecting the
argument that statements admitted under
s. 715.1
violate
minimum constitutional standards protected by
s. 7
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and particularly "the
common law `rule' against the admission of prior consistent
statements", Doherty J.A. stated at p. 255:

In my opinion, the common law position which generally
rejects evidence of a prior consistent statement made by a
witness is not founded on any principle unique to prior
consistent statements, but on the very practical assessment
that generally speaking such evidence will not provide
sufficient assistance to the trier of fact to warrant its
admission. The common law starts from the premise that
evidence of prior consistent statements made by witnesses is,
at worst, irrelevant and, at best, superfluous. Where,
however, circumstances render evidence of prior consistent
statements of potential significance to the trier of fact,
either with respect to the credibility of the declarant/
witness or with respect to a fact in issue, the common law
admits those statements.

Looking back at the excerpts from the transcript in the case
on appeal set out as Parts I and II above, it seems to me that
by and large they meet the criteria of narrative. I
specifically exclude the double hearsay as to what the
complainant said as to what her father said to her mother and I
would also exclude the statements made by the complainant to
her Grade 5 teacher and a school friend in Saskatchewan. The
latter statements neither advance nor enlarge upon the
narrative, and their introduction into evidence would only give
rise to investigations into side issues and detract from the
focus of the complainant's testimony. However, I would admit
the balance of the statements. The story that unfolds in this
case is that of a vulnerable child who has been sexually
abused, has been physically abused as a disciplinary matter,
has seen her mother assaulted by her tormentor, and has been
threatened with injury if she complains about the sexual
assaults. She had every reason to believe that the appellant
would carry out his threats. This explains her early silence.
After her mother separated from the appellant and she returned
to the west and her father, we have her account of how she had
trouble dealing with the knowledge of what she had been
subjected to and had difficulty in discussing the matter with
her father from whom she had become estranged. With a proper
limiting instruction to the jury, I think that this evidence
was properly admissible as part of the unfolding of events from
the alleged offences to the inception of this prosecution.

However, there was no such limiting instruction in this case.
The jury was never told that the complaints were not admissible
for the truth of their contents, and that they were to consider
only the fact that the complaints were made to assist them in
their understanding of what occurred and why. It is to be noted
that, in his initial ruling, the trial judge stated: "[i]f
there are any problems I can discuss that issue in my jury
charge". In fact, he did not say anything by way of a limiting
instruction with respect to either the evidence of prior
consistent statements or the evidence of emotional upset on the
part of the complainant. Despite the lack of objection of
defence counsel, this remains a most serious matter of non-
direction because the content of the statements could be
perceived by the jury as corroboration of the complainant's
story. As this court said in R. v. Lajoie (unreported judgment,
Ontario Court of Appeal, released February 23, 1993) at pp.
5-6:

In our opinion the trial judge was right in admitting the
evidence but, with respect, not as a prior consistent
statement to rebut an allegation of recent fabrication. The
evidence was admissible as evidence of the fact that the
complainant had complained, an act consistent with her story.
The defence was an all out attack on credibility and in the
circumstances, evidence of complaint or the absence of
complaint, is relevant and admissible. In addition, in the
circumstances, it was open to the Crown to lead evidence as
to reason for the complainant's reluctance and hesitation in
complaining:  see R. v. Timm [supra]; R. v. McBirnie, a
judgment of this court released November 16, 1992, per
Doherty J.A.; R v. H.P. a judgment of Salhany J., Ont. Gen.
Div., released July 14, 1992 [
1992 CanLII 15049 (ON CTGD)
, 15 C.R. (4th) 121].

Even though he had treated the evidence as a prior
consistent statement there was nothing in the charge by way
of instruction as to its limited evidentiary value. Nor was
such an instruction asked for by either party. Indeed there
was no objection to the charge which recounted the position
of the Crown and the defence, and then reviewed the evidence
of each of the witnesses. Whether viewed as a prior
consistent statement or a complaint, the evidence in question
was not evidence of the truth of the facts stated by the
complainant in her testimony. But left as it was the jury may
well have used the evidence for the very purpose they were
not to use it, a form of self-corroboration. The jury should
have been told that the evidence could not be used as proof
of the truth of the facts stated but was evidence of the fact
that she had complained and so, depending on the view the
jury took of that evidence, conduct consistent with her
story. There was non-direction amounting to misdirection.

(Emphasis added)

To summarize. Recent complaint evidence is not admissible at
the instance of the Crown as an exception to the rule against
prior consistent statements unless and until the accused raises
the issue of recent fabrication. Then, and only then, evidence
of the fact of prior consistent statements is admissible to
rebut this attack. The Crown can, however, lead evidence of
prior consistent statements as part of the res gestae (a
limited tool) or as part of the narrative. To qualify as
narrative, the witness must recount relevant and essential
facts which describe and explain his or her experience as a
victim of the crime alleged so that the trier of fact will be
in a position to understand what happened and how the matter
came to the attention of the proper authorities. In all cases
where evidence is admitted under the rubric of prior consistent
statements, the trial judge is obliged to instruct the jury as
to the limited value of the evidence. The fact that the
statements were made is admissible to assist the jury as to the
sequence of events from the alleged offence to the prosecution
so that they can understand the conduct of the complainant and
assess her truthfulness. However, the jury must be instructed
that they are not to look to the content of the statements as
proof that a crime has been committed.

Issue 2. Evidence of the complainant's emotional upset

Defence counsel objected to this category of evidence at the
same time as he made his application for a mistrial with
respect to the previous consistent statement evidence. The
trial judge dealt with this issue in the following way:

There is also an objection by the defence that there is
evidence by the complainant as to the effects of the alleged
sexual assault. The defence position, as I understand it,
that evidence can only be given by an expert for what
inferences may be drawn. I rule that the evidence of the
complainant with respect to the effect upon her of the
alleged sexual assault is properly admissible as direct
evidence of the complainant. Sexual assault is an offence
which involves far more than merely the physical aspects of
whatever alleged assault took place.

Sexual assault is an attack on the sexual integrity of the
complainant. The sexual integrity of the complainant has been
violated.

For those reasons I find that the effect upon the victim of
an alleged sexual assault is relevant evidence and is
properly admitted.

My first observation about the four episodes of apparent
emotional upset is that there is nothing in the episodes to
connect them with the sexual assaults. Worse, in the case of
episode (b), where the complainant said something which
prompted her aunt to respond "some things shouldn't be allowed
to happen" and that the complainant would be safe, the words of
the complainant were not related to the jury. We do not know if
she complained about the physical abuse she received from the
appellant as a discipline, any physical abuse her mother
received at the hands of the appellant, the sexual abuse which
the complainant now alleges, or if she had talked about any
other matter that upset her. The aunt appears to have done
nothing constructive in response to her niece's statements,
which could indicate that the complaint might have been
unrelated to sexual abuse. However, the jury was left to
imagine the worst.

The trial judge ruled that the complainant's emotional state
was relevant because it showed the effect on the complainant of
the sexual assault. The complainant did not so testify nor did
anyone else. There is no nexus between the sexual assaults and
the mood changes described in the evidence. How many of these
mood changes are natural in the childhood of any young person
and how many are attributable to a child trapped in a
relationship between her mother and a man she simply did not
like, is left to the conjecture of the jury. I think they
deserved more help. I think that it was incumbent upon the
Crown to lead an expert witness who would be in a position to
relate the emotional trauma, if such it was, to the sexual
assaults alleged. Left the way it was, it was of no probative
value and was highly prejudicial to the appellant.

Once again, there was no direction from the trial judge as to
what use the jury could make of this evidence despite the
closing argument of the Crown in which he declaimed at length
the emotional condition of the complainant as seen through the
eyes of her family. He relied strongly on the evidence of the
aunt. Crown counsel described the girl as scared and terrified.
He concluded on this issue:

Her integrity has been violated and she has been demeaned.
She is not going to get over it. She told you she is seeing a
therapist. She has been seeing a therapist for eight months.
It's not going to go away next week, two weeks from now, a
month from now. Perhaps ever. You wouldn't wish that
behaviour on your worst enemy.

On appeal, Crown counsel submitted that evidence of physical
injury and hysteria have always been admissible in rape cases,
and that emotional upset is in the same category. I think this
ignores the fact that the hysteria in the cases he referred to
was always contemporaneous with the rape or other sexual
assault. It was introduced as corroborative of the truth of the
complainant's claim that she was raped or sexually assaulted.
For example, in the case under appeal, the fact of the bruising
to the complainant's eye was admissible because the complainant
related it to the slap of the appellant which overcame her
resistance to the sexual assault. Absent such a nexus, the mere
fact that a child had an unexplained bruise would not be
admissible.

In R. v. B.(G.),
1990 CanLII 7308 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 30, 56 C.C.C. (3d) 200,
Wilson J. stated that evidence of an expert as to the
psychological and physical conditions which frequently arise as
the result of sexual abuse is admissible to provide assistance
to the trier of fact as to whether an assault has occurred (p.
55 S.C.R., p. 220 C.C.C.). In my opinion such evidence is not
only admissible, but in a case like the one under appeal, it is
mandatory if the Crown intends to rely upon lay descriptions of
the complainant's emotional condition as direct evidence that
she was subject to a sexual assault. Without such evidence,
there is nothing to connect the emotional condition described
to the offence charged as opposed to some other unhappiness
experienced by the complainant. There is nothing to demonstrate
that these four unrelated episodes and the ex post facto
recollections of the parents of the child as to her general
lassitude and sleeplessness are even manifestations of a child
with serious emotional problems. Certainly, nobody at the time
thought enough of the symptoms to consider helping her. The
complainant instituted her own therapy through a counsellor at
school in Saskatchewan.

Issue 3. Lack of instruction with respect to evidence of bad
character

With respect to this issue, the appellant submits that the
evidence of the appellant's physical abuse of the complainant's
mother was inadmissible. This evidence was clearly admissible
because it was witnessed by the complainant and was one reason
given by her as justifying her fear of the appellant and her
resultant silence about his abuse to her. There should,
however, have been a limiting instruction to the jury that this
evidence should not be relied upon as proof that the appellant
was the sort of person who would commit the offence charged and
on that basis infer that the appellant was in fact guilty: see
R. v. B.(F.F.),
1993 CanLII 167 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 697 at pp. 707-08, 79 C.C.C.
(3d) 112 at p. 119.

There is another matter relating to character evidence which
causes me concern. It relates to an attack made by Crown
counsel on the character evidence of a Dr. Spinner who was
called by the defence. Dr. Spinner had been a professor of
psychiatry at McMaster University for 20 years. He was a
neighbour of the appellant at the time of the incidents
complained of and he gave impressive character evidence on
behalf of the appellant. He also stated that the complainant
played with his own daughter, Ruth, who was about the same age.
Their playing together became less frequent after the first few
months from the time the complainant moved in with her mother
and the appellant.

In cross-examining Dr. Spinner, Crown counsel stated:

Q. I do not wish to be offensive, sir, but I am led to
believe that the reason [the complainant] was not
permitted to continue playing with Ruth was that Mr.
Fair did not want [the complainant] playing with a
Jewish girl. Would that surprise you?

A. I would be shocked if that were true.

There was no follow-up of this remark. No attempt was made by
the Crown to establish through the complainant or the appellant
that such an instruction had ever been given. Nor could there
have been on this collateral issue. This statement by Crown
counsel was, in the vernacular, a "cheap shot". It is not even
a question. It is a statement by the Crown that is completely
unsupported by the record. Crown counsel then asked the witness
if this news would surprise him knowing full well that it was
highly unlikely that Dr. Spinner would have volunteered to be a
character witness for the appellant if the statement was true
and he had known of it. I am becoming increasingly concerned
about the tendency of some trial counsel to throw out
allegations in cross-examination which they make no attempt to
substantiate. In this case, the statement in question raised a
poisonous side issue which in no way was relevant to the
charges against the appellant.

Unfortunately, the trial judge did not help matters. In his
charge to the jury, he properly instructed them that there was
not a shred of evidence to support this statement. However, he
then gave some measure of respectability to what was done by
the Crown by stating "in my view discrimination is violence"
(my emphasis). This was a case about violence in the sense
that the jury would understand it. Violence against a child and
her mother. It had nothing to do with discrimination (if that
is indeed violence) against a neighbour. The gratuitous and
unsubstantiated smear of the appellant by Crown counsel should
have been condemned by the trial judge, not treated as a
relevant line of inquiry which fell short of being fruitful.

CONCLUSION

As must be apparent from the above reasons, I am far from
satisfied that the trial judge's instructions to the jury were
adequate. The cumulative effect of the non-directions amounted
to misdirection. I would allow the appeal, set aside the
conviction, and order a new trial. In light of my proposed
disposition, I do not have to deal with the sentence appeal.

Appeal allowed.
